desc:
A partition of n into k parts is a way of writing n as a sum of exactly k positive integers where the order does not matter (so 1 + 2 + 2 and 2 + 1 + 2 are the same partition).

Return the number of such partitions, modulo 1,000,000,007. If no partition exists the answer is 0.

n = 5, k = 2  -> 2    (4+1, 3+2)
n = 7, k = 3  -> 4    (5+1+1, 4+2+1, 3+3+1, 3+2+2)
n = 4, k = 5  -> 0
hints: Count partitions without caring about order by always writing the parts in non-increasing order. Consider the smallest part of a partition.
If the smallest part equals 1, delete it: you get a partition of n - 1 into k - 1 parts. Otherwise every part is at least 2, so subtract 1 from each part.
p(n, k) = p(n - 1, k - 1) + p(n - k, k), with p(0, 0) = 1. Only the previous row of k is needed, so a rolling array over k works.
editorial: Let p(s, j) be the number of partitions of s into exactly j parts. Split the partitions by their smallest part. If the smallest part is 1, removing it leaves any partition of s - 1 into j - 1 parts, and this correspondence is reversible, giving p(s - 1, j - 1). If the smallest part is at least 2, subtract one from every part: this gives a partition of s - j into j parts, again reversibly, giving p(s - j, j). So p(s, j) = p(s - 1, j - 1) + p(s - j, j), with p(0, 0) = 1.

The second term is an unbounded-knapsack style step: it re-uses the same row j, which is why it can be computed in increasing order of s within one row. Iterate j from 1 to k and keep only the previous row. Time is O(n · k), space O(n). Because the number of partitions grows very fast, the answer is taken modulo 1,000,000,007.
